title: India's pulses imports jump 59% as masoor buying more than triples
subtitle: Fears of a weak monsoon pushed traders to buy cheaper masoor and yellow peas from Australia, Russia and Canada between April and September 2026.
content_html:
Picture a sack of masoor dal at your local kirana shop. Those lentils may well have crossed an ocean: India buys lentils from Australia, Russia and Canada. On 20 November 2026, data from the pulses traders' group IPGA, reported by The Economic Times, showed that India bought about 59% more pulses from abroad between April and September 2026 than in the same months a year earlier.

Pulses are the dried seeds we turn into dal: tur, masoor, chana, urad, moong and peas. Masoor imports grew the fastest, by 235%. That is more than three times last year's amount.

How big is the jump?

The same report gives the numbers dal by dal:

  • Masoor (lentils): up 235%
  • Chana: up 136%
  • Yellow peas: up 84%
  • Tur: up 8%
  • Urad: down 3%

The total went up about 59% by weight and about 50% by value. Value means the money paid. India spent Rs 13,649 crore on imported pulses in these six months, compared with Rs 9,133 crore in the same six months of 2025. That is Rs 4,516 crore more.

Wait, does India not grow its own dal?

It does, more than any other country. A Free Press Journal analysis from April 2026 calls India the world's largest producer, processor, importer and consumer of pulses. So India grows the most and also buys the most.

Think of a family that grows vegetables in its backyard. In a good year, the garden feeds everyone. In a bad year, someone still has to go to the sabzi market. India's dal works the same way.

The same analysis says India's pulses harvest slipped from 27.3 million tonnes in 2021 to 2022 to an estimated 26.0 million tonnes in 2025 to 2026. Imports went the other way. They rose from 2.5 million tonnes in 2022 to 2023 to a record 7.2 million tonnes in 2024 to 2025, then eased to about 5.8 million tonnes in 2025 to 2026.

Why the sudden rush this year?

The short answer is weather worries. According to ET, traders feared El Nino would hurt India's own dal crop. El Nino is a warming of the Pacific Ocean that often means weaker rain in India. Less rain means fewer pulses in Indian fields.

The fear was not empty. The report says the kharif (monsoon season) tur crop is likely to fall because of a delayed monsoon and drought in Maharashtra, Karnataka and Telangana. Sowing of rabi (winter season) chana is also behind last year.

There is a timing story too. A pulses trading broker told ET that tur and urad prices had climbed again from January 2026, which made lentils look cheap. Traders booked lentils abroad between January and March, and those ships reached India between May and July. So the jump in the April to September data also reflects choices made months earlier.

The great dal swap

Here is the clever part. The pulses that grew fastest, masoor and yellow peas, are cheaper stand-ins for tur and chana. ET says imported green lentils usually replace tur dal in south India, and yellow peas replace desi chana when mills make besan (chana flour).

It is like a canteen that runs out of paneer and serves aloo instead. The plate still looks full, and the bill stays lower. ET says this swap happens mostly in food eaten outside the home.

An official of a Tamil Nadu pulses traders' body told ET: "Masoor is currently the most affordable dal available in the market." The same report says the Tamil Nadu civil supplies department now buys imported green lentils instead of tur dal for ration shops.

Where does the dal come from?

India buys chana from Australia, yellow peas from Russia, Ukraine and Canada, and lentils from Australia, Russia and Canada, the ET report says.

Canada is a big name here. A September 2026 report by the farm research firm UkrAgroConsult says Canada shipped more than 570,000 tonnes of lentils to India in the first half of 2026. It also says India may import 1.6 million tonnes of lentils in the 2026 to 2027 season, close to the record of 1.68 million tonnes in 2023 to 2024, and that India's total pulses imports could cross 6 million tonnes this season.

What is the government doing?

The government is trying to keep dal prices calm. In May 2026, Down To Earth reported that the Centre had extended duty-free imports of yellow peas and urad until 31 March 2027. Duty is a tax paid at the border. No duty means imported dal lands cheaper.

Lentils are treated differently. UkrAgroConsult says the basic import duty on lentils stood at 10% in autumn 2026.

The ET report adds that the Centre has made stock disclosure compulsory for the pulses trade. That means traders must tell the government how much dal they are holding, so nobody can quietly hide sacks to push prices up. Tamil Nadu has put forward a limit on how much a trader can store, and the rules for chana auctions from the government's own stock have been tightened.

What this means for your dal bowl

For a home kitchen, the swap can be good news. When tur gets costly, cheaper masoor from abroad gives families and dhabas another choice, so a pot of dal does not suddenly become a luxury.

There is another side. The Down To Earth report notes that some traders warn repeated duty-free imports could hurt India's goal of growing all the pulses it needs. If cheap imports keep prices low, Indian farmers may move to other crops.

So every bowl of dal sits on a balance. Cheap imports help buyers today. Fair prices help farmers grow more tomorrow. This India Today Global video reports on India considering cuts in import duties on pulses to cool prices.
